source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
finding: First end-to-end LLM pipeline: idea, code, experiment, paper, then automated review. Cost is low, quality is uneven.
numbers: About $10-15 per paper. Review costs $0.25-0.50 each. Automated reviewer: human-level AUC 0.65 (same as humans) and F1 0.57 vs 0.49 for humans when thresholded at score 6; accuracy below the 73% reported for human reviewers.
quote: developed into a full paper at a meager cost of less than $15 per paper
limits: Template-bound tasks (small ML codebases). Authors report hallucinated plots, ablation tables and hardware facts. Reviewer is itself an LLM.
agent_relevance: Pipeline shape matches our states (idea, check, write). Their own failures (invented results) back G2/G3: results must come from executed output.

source: Beel, Kan, Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist for Autonomous Research
finding: Independent test of the AI Scientist. Many ideas were not novel, many experiments broke, papers were thin.
numbers: 5 of 12 experiments (42%) failed from coding errors. Each iteration added only 8% more code characters. Median 5 citations per paper; only 5 of 34 citations from 2020 or later. Micro-batching for SGD was labelled novel.
quote: five out of twelve proposed experiments (42%) failed due to coding errors
limits: Small sample (12 experiments); one student did the setup; older model version.
agent_relevance: Novelty checking by keyword search is weak. A novelty check needs a real literature step, not a model guess (G2, G3).

source: Yamada et al. (2025) The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search
finding: Removes human templates; adds a manager agent and tree search over experiments. One fully AI-written paper passed workshop review.
numbers: One manuscript averaged reviewer score 6.33 (about top 45% of submissions) at an ICLR workshop; it reported a negative result for compositional regularization.
quote: one manuscript achieved an average reviewer score of 6.33
limits: Workshop bar, not main conference. Authors own review found weak justification, figure-caption errors and dataset overlap.
agent_relevance: Tree search over attempts with a manager that picks branches is close to our program-controlled loop. Selection came from measured results, not self-judgement.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert review of 49 human ideas vs 49 Claude-3.5 ideas vs 49 AI ideas reranked by humans. AI ideas rated more novel, slightly less feasible.
numbers: Novelty mean (1-10): human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI+human rerank 5.81; p<0.05 under three tests with multiple-hypothesis correction. Overall: human 4.69, AI 4.83 (p=1.00 vs human), rerank 5.32 (p=0.06). Feasibility: human 6.53, AI 6.30.
quote: AI ideas are judged as significantly more novel than human ideas (p < 0.05)
limits: Ideas written to one format; reviewer agreement only 56.1%; judged before any execution; novelty is a human opinion.
agent_relevance: Novelty gain is real in rating but overall quality gain is not significant. Do not treat model novelty as proof of value.

source: Si et al. (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas - diversity and self-evaluation findings
finding: Two agent failures: generating many ideas gives mostly duplicates, and LLM judges cannot rank ideas.
numbers: After dedup at cosine 0.8, only about 5% of seed ideas were unique; unique ideas saturate as more are generated. Best LLM evaluator (Claude-3.5 pairwise ranker) 53.3% accuracy vs human inter-reviewer 56.1%. Claude-3.5 zero-shot predicts accepted vs rejected ICLR papers 71.4%; GPT-4o 61.1%; Claude-3-Opus 63.5%; few-shot and CoT gave no significant gain.
quote: increasing the number of generated ideas simply leads to repeating duplicate ideas
limits: One topic set (7 NLP topics); one generation pipeline.
agent_relevance: Supports G4 (samples from one model are not independent) and G1/G2 (no self-grading without a check). Sampling more hypotheses has a hard ceiling.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: 43 experts each spent over 100 hours executing randomly assigned human or AI ideas. After execution, the AI novelty advantage vanished and sometimes flipped.
numbers: Score change after execution (1-10): human novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052; AI novelty -1.049, excitement -1.760, effectiveness -1.879. AI drops larger on all four metrics (p<0.05).
quote: the scores of the LLM-generated ideas decrease significantly more than expert-written ideas on all evaluation metrics
limits: Only 43 projects; NLP prompting ideas only; executors may differ in skill.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G3: judging an idea before it is run is unreliable. Value must come from executed, held-out checks.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist
finding: Multi-agent generate, debate, rank (Elo tournament), evolve loop on Gemini 2.0. Elo of hypotheses rose with more compute; experts preferred its outputs.
numbers: Elo measured over 203 research goals; top-10 average and best Elo rose across time buckets. On 11 expert-evaluated goals: mean preference rank 2.36, novelty 3.64/5, impact 3.09/5, preferred over Gemini 2.0 Pro/Flash Thinking and o1. Wet-lab validation in AML drug repurposing, liver fibrosis targets, and cf-PICI mechanism.
quote: These evaluations reflect subjective expert assessments, not objective ground truth.
limits: Elo is an LLM-judged metric, not ground truth; small expert sample; goals picked by the team; Google authors.
agent_relevance: Tournament ranking and evolve step are an operator pattern we could copy, but its judge is a model, so G1/G4 warn about self-preference.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: Towards Data-Driven Discovery with Large Language Models
finding: Benchmark of data-driven discovery tasks with facet-based scoring (context, variables, relation). Agents fail most tasks.
numbers: Best system scores 25% (hypothesis match score, GPT-4 evaluator). Tested CodeGen, ReAct, DataVoyager, Reflexion and NoDataGuess baselines.
quote: even the best system scores only 25%
limits: Scoring uses a GPT-4 judge; tasks derived from published papers (contamination risk).
agent_relevance: Open-ended hypothesis search over real data is hard; reflection-style scaffolds gave only small gains.

source: Chen et al. (2025) ScienceAgentBench: Toward Rigorous Assessment of Language Agents for Data-Driven Scientific Discovery
finding: 102 tasks from 44 papers in four fields, validated by 9 experts. Agents write one Python program per task.
numbers: Best agent solves 32.4% alone and 34.3% with expert knowledge (3 attempts each). o1-preview with direct prompting and self-debug reaches 42.2% at more than 10x cost. Compared direct prompt, OpenHands CodeAct, and self-debug on 5 LLMs.
quote: the best-performing agent can only solve 32.4% of the tasks independently
limits: Programs only; success rate depends on valid execution; scoring uses output matching.
agent_relevance: Self-debug on real execution errors helped (G2); more thinking compute bought gains at high cost.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SR: Scientific Equation Discovery via Programming with Large Language Models
finding: LLM proposes equation skeletons as Python code; optimizer fits parameters; results fed back through an evolutionary buffer. Beat classic symbolic regression baselines.
numbers: Used GPT-3.5-turbo and Mixtral-8x7B; better NMSE in-domain and out-of-domain than baselines on 4 custom problems (physics, biology, materials). On Feynman problems it reached low error in under 20 iterations, which the authors read as recitation.
quote: suggesting a recitation of memorized information rather than a process of discovery
limits: Only four custom problems; synthetic modifications to known physics.
agent_relevance: Clean split of roles: model proposes structure, program fits and scores. Exactly our rule that the program checks, the model fills slots.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: A New Benchmark for Scientific Equation Discovery with LLMs
finding: 239 problems built to defeat memorization (transformed known equations and synthetic ones). Best methods score low.
numbers: Best system 31.5% symbolic accuracy on LSR-Transform and 28.1% on LSR-Synth. Symbolic accuracy correlates with out-of-domain accuracy. LaSR best numeric accuracy; LLM-SR (GPT-4o-mini) best symbolic accuracy on LSR-Transform, ranking flips on LSR-Synth.
quote: the best-performing system so far achieves only 31.5% symbolic accuracy
limits: Symbolic match judged by GPT-4o (94.6% agreement with humans on a sample).
agent_relevance: Gap between recall of famous laws and real discovery. Our tests must use novel or mutated items (G3).

source: Novikov et al. / Google DeepMind (2025) AlphaEvolve: A coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery
finding: LLM ensemble mutates programs; automatic evaluators score them; evolutionary database selects. Found real improvements.
numbers: On over 50 open math problems: matched best known on 75%, beat state of the art on 20%. 4x4 complex-valued matrix multiplication in 48 scalar multiplications (first gain over Strassen in 56 years in this setting). Kissing number in 11 dimensions improved to 593. A scheduling heuristic recovers on average 0.7% of Google fleet compute.
quote: matches the best known constructions on 75% of them
limits: Only tasks with a cheap, machine-checkable score. The 4x4 result needs complex numbers.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that LLM proposal plus exact checker finds new things. Supports program-run evaluation as the engine, not model judgement.

source: Romera-Paredes et al. (2023) Mathematical discoveries from program search with large language models (FunSearch), Nature
finding: Predecessor of AlphaEvolve: LLM writes functions, evaluator scores, island database keeps best. Improved cap set lower bounds.
numbers: Not read this session. From memory only: cap set in dimension 8 of size 512 vs prior 496. Verify before use.
limits: Unverified numbers.
agent_relevance: Same split: model proposes, checker decides.

source: Schmidgall and Moor (2025) AgentRxiv: Towards Collaborative Autonomous Research
finding: Agent labs share reports on a preprint server. Labs that read prior reports improve faster.
numbers: On MATH-500, access to prior research gave 11.4% relative improvement over baseline; multiple labs sharing gave 13.7%. Best strategy generalized to other benchmarks by 3.3% on average.
quote: 11.4% relative improvement over baseline on MATH-500
limits: Gains are in prompting methods on benchmarks the lab can overfit; no human novelty check.
agent_relevance: Memory of prior attempts (a notebook) helps. Fits the multiplayer idea of people findings read by agents.

source: Yang et al. (2025) AI Scientists Fail Without Strong Implementation Capability
finding: Position paper: the bottleneck of AI scientists is carrying out and verifying experiments, not generating ideas.
numbers: 28 papers from 5 systems scored by DeepReviewer-14B: ratings 2.33 to 4.63 (AI Scientist 3.35, v2 3.75, CycleResearcher 4.63, HKUSD 2.57), all decisions reject. Benchmarks cited: PaperBench 26% (o1-high), MLE-bench 16.9%, CORE-Bench 55.56%, SciReplicate 39%; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 1.8% on PaperBench in one run.
quote: fundamental bottleneck for AI Scientists lies in their capability to execute the requisite verification procedures
limits: Position paper; judge is an LLM; public papers may be curated.
agent_relevance: Same message as c06: put effort into checking and execution (G2, G3).

source: Chan et al. (2025) MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering
finding: 75 Kaggle competitions. Scaffold and attempts matter a lot.
numbers: o1-preview with AIDE reaches bronze medal level or better in 16.9%; pass@8 gives 34.1% (double pass@1). GPT-4o: 8.7% with 24 hours vs 11.8% with 100 hours.
quote: achieves at least the level of a Kaggle bronze medal in 16.9% of competitions
limits: Kaggle tasks with clear scores; contamination tested but not excluded.
agent_relevance: Repeated attempts with a real score beat single tries: supports best-of-N with a true check, not voting.

source: Mitchener et al. (2025) Kosmos: An AI Scientist for Autonomous Discovery
finding: Long runs (up to 12 hours, 20 cycles) with a shared world model linking data-analysis and literature agents. Every claim cites code or a paper.
numbers: Average per run: 42,000 lines of code, 1,500 papers read, 200 agent rollouts. 79.4% of 102 sampled statements judged accurate by scientists; data analysis 85% (n=55), literature 82.1% (n=28), synthesis 57.9%. Collaborators said a 20-cycle run equals about 6 months of work; findings scale linearly with cycles. Seven discoveries, three reproduced unpublished work.
quote: Independent scientists found 79.4% of statements in Kosmos reports to be accurate
limits: Only 102 statements from 3 reports; company authors; time-saved estimates are subjective.
agent_relevance: Interpretation, not execution, is the weak link (57.9%). A traceable world model per claim matches G2.

source: Toyooka et al. (2026) Jr. AI Scientist and Its Risk Report
finding: Agent that extends a real baseline paper using coding agents. Better DeepReviewer scores than earlier automated systems but real limits in author review.
numbers: Submission was rejected from Agents4Science. Higher DeepReviewer scores than earlier systems (exact values not extracted this session).
limits: Reviewer is an LLM; exact numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Its risk list (overclaiming, fabrication) is a checklist for our guardrails.

source: Udrescu and Tegmark (2020) AI Feynman: a physics-inspired method for symbolic regression
finding: Non-LLM machine scientist: neural fitting plus physics tricks (symmetry, separability, dimension analysis) applied recursively.
numbers: Solves all 100 Feynman Lectures equations; previous best software solved 71. On a harder bonus set success rose from 15% to 90%.
quote: it discovers all of them, while previous publicly available software cracks only 71
limits: Known equations; low noise; LLMs later shown to have memorized the same set (c10).
agent_relevance: Symmetry and separability checks are generic held-out tests (G3) a thinking schema could use.

source: Cranmer (2023) Interpretable Machine Learning for Science with PySR and SymbolicRegression.jl
finding: Open-source evolutionary symbolic regression library used as the standard baseline in LLM equation work.
numbers: Downloaded, not read this session.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Baseline for any equation-discovery test.

source: Langley, Simon, Bradshaw, Zytkow (1987) Scientific Discovery: Computational Explorations of the Creative Processes (BACON)
finding: Early heuristic discovery programs (BACON and kin) rediscovered Kepler and Ohm style laws by search over data with fixed heuristics.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Rediscovery of known laws, as with the Feynman set later.
agent_relevance: Same recitation-vs-discovery question as c10, c11.

source: King et al. (2009) The automation of science (Adam robot scientist), Science
finding: Robot Adam formed and tested hypotheses about yeast gene function with lab automation and logic-based reasoning.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Closed loop with a real experiment is the old, working form of G3.

source: Cross-reading: c04, c06, c12
finding: Pattern across the studies: judgement of an unrun idea favours the LLM; after execution the gap closes; wins come where an exact checker exists (AlphaEvolve).
numbers: c04 novelty +0.80 for AI before execution; c06 AI drops 1.05 to 1.88 points after; c12 20% of 50+ problems beaten with exact scoring.
limits: Synthesis by this agent from three sources, not a new study.
agent_relevance: Core design rule: rank hypotheses by executed, held-out checks; use model judgement only to break ties, never alone.

source: Cross-reading: c10, c11, c19
finding: Recitation confound: LLM discovery systems look strong on famous equations and weak on transformed or synthetic ones.
numbers: c11 best 31.5% and 28.1% symbolic accuracy on transformed/synthetic problems; c19 100/100 on Feynman for a non-LLM method; c10 low error under 20 iterations on Feynman.
limits: Synthesis by this agent.
agent_relevance: Any test of our agent in a science-like domain needs mutated items so recall cannot pass.

source: Cross-reading: c01, c02, c15, c18
finding: Automated reviewers and self-reviews flatter AI-written papers; independent checks find execution errors, hallucinated results and thin citation.
numbers: c02 42% experiment failures; c15 all 28 papers reject-level by DeepReviewer; c01 hallucinated plots and tables; c18 rejected by Agents4Science.
limits: Synthesis; small samples.
agent_relevance: Add a rule: every number in an output must trace to executed code (extends G2).

source: Cross-reading: c14, c16, c17
finding: Memory and iteration helped: prior-report access (c14, +11.4%), pass@8 doubling pass@1 (c16), findings scaling linearly with cycles (c17).
numbers: c14 11.4% and 13.7% relative; c16 16.9% to 34.1%; c17 linear to 20 cycles.
limits: Synthesis; benchmarks differ and gains may saturate (idea duplicates in c05).
agent_relevance: Budgeted repeat attempts with a notebook are supported; unlimited sampling of ideas is not (c05).
